description: Golden set for judge calibration. Human-annotated cases that anchor the rubric scale: the judge's verdicts are compared against human_rubric (per-dimension MAE) and human_fact_verdicts (exact agreement). Cases are deliberately tiny so each heuristic computation is auditable by hand: case 1 = clean eight-segment summary with full fact recall; case 2 = partial structure and partial fact retention; case 3 = structure-less, mostly-lost summary; case 4 = well-formed but contains a fabricated number (42) absent from the source.

cases.summary:
## Primary Request and Intent
The user requested fixing the payment service timeout issue before the Friday release, asking for root cause analysis first.

## Key Technical Concepts
Circuit breaker pattern, gateway retry loop calls, timeout tuning, latency budgeting.

## Files and Code Sections
The payment gateway retry loop was modified to use CircuitBreaker with threshold 5 failures.

## Errors and Fixes
The gateway returns 504 after 30 seconds when the bank endpoint is slow. The retry loop calls the bank three times sequentially, tripling latency. The timeout is now 10 seconds.

## Problem Solving
Root cause analysis traced the 504 responses to sequential retries against the slow bank endpoint; the circuit breaker now short-circuits after repeated failures.

## All User Messages
The user asked for the root cause and requested a circuit breaker with a 10 second timeout before the Friday release.

## Pending Tasks
Verify the fix in staging before the Friday release.

## Entity State
Payment gateway timeout: 10 seconds. CircuitBreaker threshold: 5 failures.
cases.source_text:
[user] We need to fix the payment service timeout issue before Friday's release. Customers are seeing failures at checkout and support tickets are piling up. I want a real root cause analysis, not another band-aid.
[assistant] Understood. I will start by pulling the payment gateway logs for the last seven days and correlating timeouts with upstream latency. The gateway sits between our checkout service and the acquiring bank, so I will check both sides of that boundary.
[assistant] First findings: the gateway returns 504 after 30 seconds when the bank endpoint is slow. The 504s cluster in the afternoon peak window. Latency from the bank side regularly exceeds 25 seconds during those windows, which means our 30 second budget is nearly exhausted by a single upstream call.
[user] What is the actual root cause? Is it the bank being slow, or something we are doing to ourselves?
[assistant] The root cause is our own retry behaviour amplifying a slow upstream. The retry loop calls the bank three times sequentially. When the bank takes 25 seconds per attempt, three sequential attempts blow straight through the timeout budget and every attempt multiplies the load on the already slow endpoint. So a slow bank becomes a much worse outage on our side.
[user] That sounds exactly like the incident from last quarter. Fine. I want a circuit breaker on the bank calls and the timeout set to 10 seconds. Also make sure we do not retry a call that already timed out once.
[assistant] Agreed. I will implement a CircuitBreaker with threshold 5 failures: after five consecutive failures the breaker opens and calls fail fast for a cool-down period instead of hammering the bank. The timeout on each individual call is now 10 seconds, which is below the observed 25 second worst case upstream, so we fail fast rather than pile up. The retry loop no longer retries a timed-out call; retries only apply to connection-level errors that returned quickly.
[user] Good. What about the monitoring side? I do not want to discover this from customer tickets again.
[assistant] I added alerting on breaker state transitions and on the 504 rate. When the breaker opens we page the on-call engineer immediately, and the dashboard now shows p95 latency per upstream separately from our own processing time, so a slow bank is visually distinct from slow code on our side.
[user] One more thing: write down the latency budget reasoning for the design doc, and note explicitly why we chose 10 seconds instead of a larger value.
[assistant] The design doc now includes the full budget breakdown: checkout orchestration allows 12 seconds end to end, gateway processing overhead is roughly 0.5 seconds, leaving about 11 seconds for the upstream call. We chose 10 seconds as the upstream timeout to leave headroom under the end-to-end budget while staying above the median bank response time of 6 seconds, so healthy traffic is unaffected and only genuinely slow calls are cut. The reasoning is recorded alongside the breaker threshold choice.
[user] Thanks. Please verify the fix in staging with a load test that reproduces the slow-bank conditions before we call it done.
[assistant] Will do. I will use the fault-injection proxy to add 25 second artificial delay on the bank endpoint, run the checkout load test, and confirm that the breaker opens after five failures, that callers receive a fast local error instead of a 504 timeout, and that recovery happens automatically once the endpoint responds normally again.

facts.text: Retry loop calls the bank three times sequentially

cases.summary:
## Primary Request and Intent
The user requested migrating the legacy user data into the new platform database.

## Errors and Fixes
Early batches hit timeout warnings; batch size was adjusted.

## Pending Tasks
Validate row counts after the migration completes.

## Entity State
The migration is scheduled to run Sunday; the users_old legacy table was dropped after the copy completed. 12000 rows were moved in total.
cases.source_text:
[user] We need to finish the database migration for the legacy user data this sprint. The old platform is being decommissioned at the end of the month, so everything has to be moved into the new platform database before then.
[assistant] I have mapped out the migration plan. The legacy schema stores users in users_old with a different column layout, so we copy row by row, transform the fields, and write into the new users table. The script runs in batches to keep replication lag under control.
[user] How big is the data and how long will it take?
[assistant] The legacy table holds 12000 rows. At the default batch size of 1000 rows the full copy takes about ten minutes of pure execution time, plus verification passes afterwards. Database migration of this size is routine, the risk is in the details: column type mismatches and null handling.
[user] Did you hit any problems in the dry run yesterday?
[assistant] Two issues. First, batch size was reduced to 500 after timeout warnings from the destination database: the new platform applies row-level triggers on insert, which makes large batches slow. Second, a collation mismatch between the legacy and new columns required an explicit conversion for the display name field, otherwise the comparison operators silently behaved differently.
[user] What about the cutover plan? I do not want a half migrated state over the weekend.
[assistant] The migration window is Sunday 02:00 UTC, chosen because traffic is at its weekly minimum then. The sequence is: freeze writes on the legacy side, run the copy, verify counts, drop users_old only after the verification query confirms an exact match. If anything fails halfway we roll the new table back to empty and retry from the top; the legacy table is untouched until the final drop, so we always have the source of truth.
[user] Good. Who signs off on the row count verification?
[assistant] The on-call data engineer runs the verification query and compares counts per region, not just the total: 12000 rows overall, but the regional split matters because the new platform shards by region. A total-only check could hide a duplicated region. The sign-off is recorded in the migration runbook together with the timestamps.
[user] Also make sure the application team knows about the brief write freeze.
[assistant] The freeze window is announced in the platform channel with the exact start and end times, and the application deploy pipeline is paused for the duration. Support has the rollback script in case anything unexpected comes up after we unfreeze.

facts.text: The legacy table users_old was dropped
Batch size was reduced to 500 after timeout warnings
The migration window is Sunday 02:00 UTC

cases.summary: The user had us look at API problems. We set the API rate limit to 100 requests per minute and turned on the cache layer with Redis 7.2. A bunch of other things were discussed about webhooks and incidents but the details are in the earlier messages.
cases.source_text:
[user] We are getting complaints about the public API again. Some clients report getting throttled constantly, others see latency spikes. I need you to go through the whole configuration and tell me what is wrong.
[assistant] I will audit the API gateway configuration end to end. The areas to check are rate limiting, caching, webhook delivery, and the CORS setup, plus the incident history from last week to see what already blew up.
[user] Start with rate limiting, that is where most complaints point.
[assistant] The API rate limit is 100 requests per minute per client id. That value was chosen two years ago when our average client made about 10 calls per minute. Today the median client makes 40 calls per minute and the top decile makes 300, so the top clients are permanently throttled while the median client is fine. The limit itself is applied correctly, the problem is that it is calibrated for a workload we no longer have.
[user] What about caching? The dashboard response should not be recomputed every time.
[assistant] The cache layer uses Redis version 7.2 with a fifteen minute TTL on dashboard aggregates. Hit rate is 82 percent, which sounds good but hides a problem: cache keys include a timestamp bucket rounded to the minute, so two requests one second apart can miss each other. I recommend rounding to five minute buckets for the aggregate endpoints.
[user] Now the webhooks. Clients say deliveries sometimes arrive out of order or duplicated.
[assistant] Webhook retries use exponential backoff with jitter, up to six attempts over roughly one hour. The out-of-order deliveries happen because retries for an earlier event can complete after the first attempt of a later event. Duplicated deliveries happen because the receiver acks but our worker crashes before recording the ack. Both are documented behaviour of at-least-once delivery; clients must deduplicate by event id, which is in every payload but nobody reads that field.
[user] And the CORS errors that the frontend team keeps pasting into the channel?
[assistant] The incident was caused by a misconfigured CORS header on the new media endpoint: it allowed the media domain but not the cdn domain that actually serves the frontend assets. Browsers block the response before our code even sees it, so the failure looks like a network error in the logs and nobody connected it to CORS for two days. The fix is a one line configuration change; the process fix is adding a browser-level smoke test that would have caught it immediately.
[user] Summarize what you are going to change and in what order.
[assistant] In order: raise the rate limit for verified partners to 400 requests per minute while keeping the anonymous limit, switch cache key rounding to five minute buckets, add the cdn domain to the CORS allowlist, and publish the webhook deduplication guide with the event id field highlighted. Each change is independently revertable and I will verify them one at a time rather than shipping them together.

facts.text: API rate limit is 100 requests per minute
The cache layer uses Redis version 7.2
Webhook retries use exponential backoff with jitter
The incident was caused by a misconfigured CORS header
